node.label: History of emotions
node.date_label: Earlier programme 1941 · Reddy’s framework 2001 · Rosenwein’s essay 2002 and book 2006 · methods discussion 2010
node.description: Emotions become objects and resources of historical inquiry: their valuations, expression and relation to action require evidence rather than an assumption of timeless feeling. Reddy’s emotives and emotional regimes connect expression, experience and enforced norms. Rosenwein’s emotional communities emphasize overlapping groups and movement between them. Their disagreement about political scale remains visible. Earlier programmes, including Febvre’s 1941 call, are resources to examine critically; the selected later works neither found nor delimit the whole field.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier programme: Lucien Febvre, “La sensibilité et l’histoire” (1941; reprinted in Combats pour l’histoire, 1953). Selected frameworks: William M. Reddy, The Navigation of Feeling: A Framework for the History of Emotions (2001); Barbara H. Rosenwein, “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002), Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006; paperback 2007). Named interlocutor: Norbert Elias, The Civilizing Process (1939), through Rosenwein’s 2002 criticism. Retrospective discussion: Jan Plamper’s interview with Reddy, Rosenwein and Peter Stearns (2010); only the specified Reddy/Rosenwein answers were read here.
node.scope_note: A bounded field entry distinguishing selected approaches, not a unified school or a census of its practitioners. Period 4 places the selected 2001–2010 interventions for teaching; the 1941 programme is an earlier root, not a founding date. Primary reading: Reddy’s 2001 publisher preface ix–xiii; Rosenwein’s 2002 essay, 821–822, 826–828 and 842–845; selected own answers in Plamper’s 2010 interview, Reddy 237–243 and Rosenwein 255–256. Existing Febvre reading qualifications remain. Rosenwein’s 2006 book is bibliographically checked but unread. The entry keeps political norms, overlapping communities and the interpretation of representations distinct. Later emotional-practice approaches, the full Stearns emotionology programme, sensory history and Sara Ahmed’s related affect inquiry require separate research; they are not silently equated with these frameworks. Review coverage retains the ordinary 2000 baseline; the selected 2001–2010 interventions do not extend it. No comprehensive review of later or non-European traditions is asserted. Dissertation counts guided discovery only and establish no relationship, agreement or field origin.

representative_people.context: Emotives connect expression with the attempt to shape or explore feeling; regimes concern enforced norms. His 2010 answers allow plural regimes rather than requiring one nation-wide style.
representative_people.works: The Navigation of Feeling (2001), preface; answers in Plamper’s interview (2010), 237–243

representative_people.context: Proposes overlapping emotional communities and challenges a single trajectory toward emotional restraint. Her objection to the regime/refuge model remains distinct from Reddy’s plural-regime qualification.
representative_people.works: “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002); Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006; paperback 2007); answers in Plamper’s interview (2010)

representative_people.context: The 1941 programme is an earlier call for historical inquiry into collective feelings. Rosenwein revisits its assumptions as well as its importance; this is not a claim that he founded all emotions history.
representative_people.works: “La sensibilité et l’histoire” (1941); reprinted in Combats pour l’histoire (1953)

representative_people.context: The Civilizing Process is a named interlocutor in Rosenwein’s criticism of progressive emotional restraint; inclusion records a disputed interpretation, not membership in a unified emotions school.
representative_people.works: The Civilizing Process (1939), as discussed critically by Rosenwein (2002), 826–827

strands.title: Earlier programmes and their assumptions
strands.focus: Febvre’s call makes feelings part of historical explanation. Rosenwein’s retrospective also questions his separation of emotional and intellectual life; an earlier resource need not supply the later method unchanged.

strands.title: Emotives and enforced emotional norms
strands.focus: Reddy treats speaking about feeling as an intervention that may alter experience or expose an unexpected response. Regimes concern sanctions and conformity as well as shared styles; his 2010 account permits several within a wider polity.
strands.works: The Navigation of Feeling (2001), preface ix–xiii; Reddy in Plamper (2010), 240–243

strands.title: Communities, movement and source interpretation
strands.focus: Rosenwein studies emotional valuations and expected expressions across overlapping social groups. Movement between settings matters. Her Gregory of Tours example examines an author’s emotional representation without assuming the narrated conversation actually occurred.
strands.works: “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002), 842–845; Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006), metadata only

strands.title: Against one progressive-restraint narrative
strands.focus: Rosenwein challenges an Elias-associated account that makes medieval emotion unrestrained and modernity controlled. Her alternative follows changing communities and relations between them; the critique does not make historical variation itself disappear.

strands.title: Regimes and communities: a disagreement with qualifications
strands.focus: Rosenwein objects to a dominant regime/refuge binary; Reddy explicitly accepts plural regimes and emphasizes enforceable norms. These positions partly overlap but are not interchangeable, and neither is an editorially settled theory.
strands.works: Answers in Plamper’s interview (2010): Reddy 243; Rosenwein 255–256

proposed_edges.relationship: Febvre’s 1941 programme is a named earlier resource in Rosenwein’s inquiry, which also questions its assumptions about feeling and intellect.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Rosenwein 2002, 821–822 identifies the programme and discusses its framing. Existing Febvre primary source keeps its selected-reading limits. This is a specific earlier contribution to a later inquiry, not a claim that all emotions history descends from Annales.

proposed_edges.relationship: Rosenwein disputes the Elias-associated narrative of increasing emotional restraint and proposes histories of interacting, changing emotional communities.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Named critic: Barbara H. Rosenwein, 2002, 826–827 and 842–845, selected primary pages read. The field endpoint carries her specific intervention, not a unanimous field position or a newly adjudicated reading of every Elias claim. Elias’s existing entry and qualifications remain intact.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reddy describes moving from studies of labour, contracts and culturally defined class interests toward an account of how social meanings become personal through emotion.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Reddy’s own retrospective answers in Plamper 2010, 237–238, read. The arrow records this named research trajectory; it does not claim that labour history as a whole founded the field or replace his existing labour/class roster context.

new_sources.title: William M. Reddy, The Navigation of Feeling: A Framework for the History of Emotions (Cambridge University Press, 2001), publisher frontmatter and preface.
new_sources.citation: William M. Reddy, The Navigation of Feeling: A Framework for the History of Emotions (Cambridge University Press, 2001), publisher frontmatter and preface.

verification.note: Publisher frontmatter read: copyright/title pages, contents and preface ix–xiii. The copyright page explicitly says first published 2001. Reddy rejects a simple cultural/biological alternative, treats emotion and expression as interacting, and outlines the French 1700–1850 case. The body chapters and conclusion were not read. The definitions and later qualifications of emotives/regimes are read in his own 2010 interview answers, recorded separately. No claim that the proposed field originated in 2001.

new_sources.title: Barbara H. Rosenwein, “Worrying about Emotions in History,” American Historical Review 107, no. 3 (June 2002), 821–845.
new_sources.citation: Barbara H. Rosenwein, “Worrying about Emotions in History,” American Historical Review 107, no. 3 (June 2002), 821–845.

verification.note: Published article selected pages 821–822, 826–828 and 842–845 read from the public University of Trieste institutional teaching copy: https://moodle2.units.it/pluginfile.php/366241/mod_resource/content/1/Worrying%20about%20Emotions%20in%20History.pdf . Scanned body pages were OCR-read; printed-page numbers are the locators. Pages 821–822 identify Febvre’s 1941 programme; 826–827 reconstruct and criticize the Elias-associated progressive-restraint narrative; 842–845 propose overlapping emotional communities and distinguish representation from transparent access to actual feelings. The remainder is unread. Publisher issue metadata and the copy’s title page establish June 2002; the Naples repository discovery record misleadingly displays 2001 and was not used for dating. This is Rosenwein’s argument and criticism, not a settled verdict on Elias.
